transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it is nice to meet you too, doctor, though I must admit I'm quite overwhelmed right now. What brings me in... well, I suppose it's the voices. I just keep hearing these very, very clear voices, and it’s becoming impossible to manage. 

I live in a fairly quiet building, you see, but lately, in my apartment, I hear them constantly. It sounds exactly like a group of women whispering right from behind the walls. Just murmuring and whispering through the drywall. And the strange thing is, it’s not just at home. I try to get out, I go to the art museums downtown because I’ve always loved the quiet there—I got my degree years ago and I've always appreciated the atmosphere—but even there, when I wander into one of those large, empty museum rooms where there's absolutely no one else around, I hear them again. The exact same women, whispering from behind the gallery walls. 

And they are so specific about what they want to say. They just keep telling me which photographs belong in the archive. Over and over, discussing this archive and dictating to me which specific photographs need to be placed in it. I try to focus on other things, I try to just sit in my living room and read, or look at the museum exhibits, but their voices are so clear, and they just won't stop whispering about the photographs and the archive... it's just exhausting, to be honest with you.
Have you been diagnosed with any brain or nervous system illness?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've seen my regular doctor for years—decades, really, ever since I moved into that quiet building I mentioned. And he always does the standard physicals, you know, checks my reflexes with that little rubber hammer, looks in my eyes with the light, and he’s never once said a single word about my brain or my nervous system being damaged. 

I don't have Parkinson's or dementia or anything of that sort. My mother, bless her heart, did have some nerve pain in her legs when she got to be about my age, but my nerves are perfectly fine. I don't get migraines, I've never had a seizure, and my memory is just as sharp as it ever was when I was getting my bachelor's degree. I still remember all the historical dates on the placards at the museum, clear as day, without even having to write them down. 

So physically, my brain is completely healthy. No doctor has ever told me otherwise. Which makes it all the more baffling, you see, because if my brain is perfectly fine and my nervous system is intact, why am I the only one who can hear them? Why are these women so fixated on me and the archive? It just doesn't make any sense if there's no physical illness, but they just keep whispering anyway...
How long have you been hearing these whispering voices?

Well, let me think back... it’s been quite a while now, hasn't it? I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time the weather was turning, and the heating pipes in my building usually make such a racket, but this... this was completely different. It has been about eight months now. Yes, eight solid months. 

I thought at first, maybe it's just the neighbors, maybe someone new moved in next door and they just talk very softly. But then it just kept going, day in and day out, every single day for the last eight months. And it's not just the whispering, doctor. For that exact same amount of time, I've had this... this absolute certainty, this undeniable knowledge that people are watching my archive. I don't know how they know about it, or how they're doing it, but they are watching it. I can feel it. 

I’ve tried to figure out how they could possibly be monitoring the photographs. I check the locks on my door, I make sure the blinds are drawn tight, especially in the evenings when the streetlights cast those long shadows into the living room, but it simply doesn't matter. For eight months, the women have been whispering, and I just *know* there are people watching the archive. It's a terrible, heavy feeling, really, knowing you're being observed like that in your own private space. And like I said, even when I go to the museum to escape it, it's the exact same feeling, the same voices, the same watching... I just can't seem to get a single moment of peace from it, not once in eight months.
Because of these experiences, has your day-to-day functioning gotten worse?

Oh, it’s completely fallen apart, doctor. Just... terribly worse. I used to be so organized, you know. I was always very involved with the local historical society and the museum boards, always the one they relied on for things. But lately, with the whispering and the constant feeling of the archive being watched... I just haven't been able to go. I’ve missed so many board meetings. It’s embarrassing, really, because I know I’ve lost the trust of my colleagues. I can just feel it; they think I'm completely unreliable now. 

And it’s not just the meetings, it’s the daily things right inside my own home. The mail comes, and I just stare at the envelopes, and... well, I've missed paying my bills. The electric, the water... I used to be so meticulous with my checkbook, balancing it to the penny every Sunday evening at my kitchen table, but now I just can't manage the money at all. I get too distracted by what the voices are dictating to me.

It actually got to the point where my cousin had to get involved. She lives a few towns over—usually we just exchange letters or Christmas cards, but she had to come down. She and... well, one of the museum administrators actually had to step in together to help me. It was quite overwhelming, having them both there, going through my mail and my calendar. They realized I couldn't manage my appointments anymore, or handle my finances, or even attend those public gallery events safely on my own. They were so worried I might get confused or overwhelmed in public, or that I wasn't safe. It’s just humiliating, honestly, to have someone else have to take over your life like that, at my age, after being independent for so long. But I just couldn't keep up with any of it, not with those women constantly whispering.
